findings.impact: Exposes such participants to a dual-track financial risk combining potentially large administrative fines with separate civil damages claims for the same incident, an exposure not disclosed by either provision read in isolation.
findings.mechanism: Article 53(4) preserves participants' civil liability under applicable Union and Member State law for harm inflicted on third parties from sandbox experimentation, operating independently of the administrative fines of up to 6% of turnover available under Article 71 for the same underlying non-compliance.

evidence.quote: Participants in the AI regulatory sandbox shall remain liable under applicable Union and Member States liability legislation for any harm inflicted on third parties as a result from the experimentation taking place in the sandbox.
administrative fines of up to 30 000 000 EUR or, if the offender is company, up to 6 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher

chains.description: Continuous real-time risk-monitoring duties on participants (I1) require hosting authorities to build matching supervisory capacity (I2); this operational load is layered with a recurring annual reporting and coordination burden to the AI Board/Commission (I4), which in turn feeds into and is partly shaped by centralized Commission implementing acts standardizing sandbox modalities across Member States (I5).

Because the personal-data reuse exception is confined to enumerated public-interest purposes (I8), only qualifying participants must then build isolated, monitored data environments (I7), operate long-tail log retention (I9) and scheduled deletion processes (I10); cumulatively this bundle of conditions produces a compliance burden that is disproportionately costly for smaller, resource-constrained participants (I13).

Small providers receive priority sandbox admission (I15), but this earlier access does not reduce the resource-intensive Art 54 operational duties that apply once inside (I18), so the aggregate compliance burden identified in I13 persists regardless of admission priority.

Tiered administrative fines apply to all providers by infringement severity (I19); statutory leniency factors requiring authorities to weigh small providers' economic viability reduce their relative exposure (I20), which correspondingly shifts a proportionately heavier turnover-based burden onto large-scale providers for equivalent infringements (I21).

Sandbox participation preserves full civil liability for third-party harm (I3); where the same underlying non-compliance also breaches the Regulation, it separately triggers administrative fines under the Art 71 tiered regime (I19), producing a combined dual-track financial exposure for the participant (I25).

disagreements.note: Legal and fiscal findings characterize Art 55(1)(a) priority sandbox access as a clear net benefit improving small providers' relative market position, while the stakeholder finding argues this priority is largely illusory in practice because it does not relieve small providers of the same resource-intensive Art 54 operational duties faced by all participants once admitted.

open_questions.question: Does the 'direct supervision and guidance' standard under Art 53 imply dedicated per-sandbox authority staffing, and how will resource-constrained Member States meet this without dedicated EU funding support?
How will Commission implementing acts under Art 53(6) interact with national sandbox schemes that are already operational before those acts are adopted?

What quantitative or qualitative threshold defines 'small-scale provider' for priority sandbox access, fee reduction, and penalty leniency purposes, and will it be applied consistently across Member States?

Will the aggregate infrastructure burden of Art 54 conditions in practice deter smaller or start-up participants from ever invoking the personal-data reuse exception, undermining the sandbox's innovation objective for that group?

How will individual Member States decide whether to apply administrative fines to public authorities under Art 71(7), and could divergent choices create a two-tier compliance regime domestically and across the Union?

Given that Art 54 permits personal-data reuse without data-subject consent, is any alternative safeguard (e.g., prior notice, opt-out, or oversight mechanism) required to compensate for the absence of consent?

board.affected_actor: providers and start-ups participating in AI regulatory sandboxes
board.impact: Participants must maintain continuous real-time risk-monitoring capacity and be ready to immediately mitigate or halt testing whenever competent authorities identify significant risks to health, safety or fundamental rights.
board.mechanism: Art 53(1) requires sandbox operation under the 'direct supervision and guidance' of competent authorities pursuant to a specific plan, and Art 53(3) requires immediate mitigation or suspension of the testing process whenever significant risks are identified.

evidence.quote: This shall take place under the direct supervision and guidance by the competent authorities with a view to ensuring compliance with the requirements of this Regulation

Any significant risks to health and safety and fundamental rights identified during the development and testing of such systems shall result in immediate mitigation and, failing that, in the suspension of the development and testing process until such mitigation takes place.

board.affected_actor: competent authorities supervising AI regulatory sandboxes
board.impact: Hosting authorities must build sufficient technical and staffing capacity to continuously monitor sandbox participants and exercise corrective powers, including suspension, in real time rather than through ex-post inspection alone.
board.mechanism: Art 53(3) expressly preserves the authorities' full supervisory and corrective powers within the sandbox and obliges them to act on any significant identified risk.

evidence.quote: The AI regulatory sandboxes shall not affect the supervisory and corrective powers of the competent authorities.

board.affected_actor: participants in AI regulatory sandboxes
board.impact: Sandbox participants retain full civil liability exposure for third-party harm arising from their experimentation, so sandbox status provides no liability shield.
board.mechanism: Art 53(4) expressly preserves participants' liability under applicable Union and Member State liability legislation for harm inflicted on third parties as a result of sandbox experimentation.

evidence.quote: Participants in the AI regulatory sandbox shall remain liable under applicable Union and Member States liability legislation for any harm inflicted on third parties as a result from the experimentation taking place in the sandbox.

board.affected_actor: Member States competent authorities operating AI regulatory sandboxes
board.impact: Hosting authorities incur a recurring annual reporting and cross-Member-State coordination burden through the Board, requiring dedicated administrative capacity beyond day-to-day supervision.
board.mechanism: Art 53(5) obliges authorities that establish sandboxes to coordinate within the European AI Board and submit annual reports to the Board and Commission on implementation results.

evidence.quote: They shall submit annual reports to the Board and the Commission on the results from the implementation of those scheme, including good practices, lessons learnt and recommendations on their setup

board.affected_actor: European Commission
board.impact: The Commission gains rule-making power to standardize sandbox eligibility, procedures and participants' rights and obligations across Member States, centralizing an element of the enforcement framework.
board.mechanism: Art 53(6) empowers the Commission to set the modalities and conditions of sandbox operation, including eligibility, application, participation and exit rules, via implementing acts.

evidence.quote: The modalities and the conditions of the operation of the AI regulatory sandboxes, including the eligibility criteria and the procedure for the application, selection, participation and exiting from the sandbox, and the rights and obligations of the participants shall be set out in implementing acts.

board.affected_actor: national data protection authorities and other competent national authorities
board.impact: These authorities acquire an active coordination duty to participate in sandbox oversight whenever personal data or their supervisory remit is engaged, rather than remaining passive observers.
board.mechanism: Art 53(2) requires Member States to ensure that national data protection authorities and other relevant national authorities are 'associated to the operation' of the sandbox.

evidence.quote: the national data protection authorities and those other national authorities are associated to the operation of the AI regulatory sandbox

board.affected_actor: sandbox participants processing personal data (data controllers)
board.impact: Only controllers able to build and continuously operate an isolated, access-controlled processing environment with active risk-monitoring and mitigation mechanisms can lawfully rely on the reuse exception, requiring new dedicated data-governance infrastructure.
board.mechanism: Art 54(1)(c) and (d) require effective monitoring and response mechanisms for fundamental-rights risks and a functionally separate, isolated and access-restricted data processing environment.

evidence.quote: any personal data to be processed in the context of the sandbox are in a functionally separate, isolated and protected data processing environment under the control of the participants and only authorised persons have access to that data

there are effective monitoring mechanisms to identify if any high risks to the fundamental rights of the data subjects may arise during the sandbox experimentation as well as response mechanism to promptly mitigate those risks

board.affected_actor: data controllers seeking to reuse personal data for AI sandbox development
board.impact: The reuse exception is narrowly available only to controllers whose AI development serves one of three enumerated public-interest areas, excluding purely commercial or other-sector innovators from this data-reuse route.
board.mechanism: Art 54(1)(a) limits eligibility to AI systems developed for safeguarding substantial public interest in criminal law enforcement/public security, public safety and health, or environmental protection.

evidence.quote: the innovative AI systems shall be developed for safeguarding substantial public interest in one or more of the following areas

the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or the execution of criminal penalties, including the safeguarding against and the prevention of threats to public security

board.affected_actor: sandbox participants processing personal data
board.impact: Participants must build and maintain a log-retention system operative for the sandbox period plus a further year, extending compliance obligations beyond the sandbox's active phase.
board.mechanism: Art 54(1)(h) requires logs of the processing of personal data to be kept for the duration of participation and one year after termination, solely for accountability and documentation purposes.

evidence.quote: the logs of the processing of personal data in the context of the sandbox are kept for the duration of the participation in the sandbox and 1 year after its termination, solely for the purpose of and only as long as necessary for fulfilling accountability and documentation obligations

board.affected_actor: sandbox participants processing personal data
board.impact: Participants must operate a scheduled data-deletion process tied to two independent triggers (end of sandbox participation or end of retention period), requiring ongoing data-lifecycle management capability.
board.mechanism: Art 54(1)(g) mandates deletion of personal data processed in the sandbox once participation terminates or the data reaches the end of its retention period.

evidence.quote: any personal data processed in the context of the sandbox are deleted once the participation in the sandbox has terminated or the personal data has reached the end of its retention period

board.affected_actor: sandbox participants processing personal data and hosting competent authorities
board.impact: Participants must maintain full audit-ready technical documentation of their training/testing rationale while authorities take on the recurring administrative task of publishing project summaries, together producing continuous documentation and transparency obligations for both sides.
board.mechanism: Art 54(1)(i) requires a complete description of the AI development process to be kept as part of Annex IV technical documentation, and (j) requires a public summary of the project to be published on the competent authority's website.

evidence.quote: complete and detailed description of the process and rationale behind the training, testing and validation of the AI system is kept together with the testing results as part of the technical documentation in Annex IV
a short summary of the AI project developed in the sandbox, its objectives and expected results published on the website of the competent authorities

board.affected_actor: sandbox participants processing personal data
board.impact: Participants must operate strict internal access barriers preventing any external transmission of the data, and must ensure sandbox processing never feeds into decisions affecting the data subjects concerned.
board.mechanism: Art 54(1)(e) prohibits transmission, transfer or access by other parties, and (f) prohibits the processing from leading to measures or decisions affecting the data subjects.

evidence.quote: any personal data processed are not be transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties
any processing of personal data in the context of the sandbox do not lead to measures or decisions affecting the data subjects

board.affected_actor: small-scale providers and start-ups
board.impact: Small providers gain a preferential admission right to sandboxes ahead of other applicants, improving their relative access to the supervised testing regime compared to larger competitors.
board.mechanism: Art 55(1)(a) requires Member States to provide small-scale providers and start-ups with priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes where they meet eligibility conditions.

evidence.quote: provide small-scale providers and start-ups with priority access to the AI regulatory sandboxes to the extent that they fulfil the eligibility conditions

board.affected_actor: small-scale providers
board.impact: Small providers are entitled to proportionately reduced conformity-assessment fees, lowering their compliance costs relative to larger providers facing standard fees.
board.mechanism: Art 55(2) requires that small-scale providers' interests and needs be taken into account when setting Article 43 conformity assessment fees, reducing those fees proportionately to their size and market size.

evidence.quote: The specific interests and needs of the small-scale providers shall be taken into account when setting the fees for conformity assessment under Article 43, reducing those fees proportionately to their size and market size.

board.affected_actor: Member States
board.impact: Member States must build ongoing outreach and support infrastructure specifically targeted at small providers and start-ups, an institutional capacity commitment distinct from general market surveillance.
board.mechanism: Art 55(1)(b) and (c) oblige Member States to organize tailored awareness-raising activities and, where appropriate, establish a dedicated communication channel for small-scale providers.

evidence.quote: organise specific awareness raising activities about the application of this Regulation tailored to the needs of the small-scale providers and users
establish a dedicated channel for communication with small-scale providers and user and other innovators to provide guidance and respond to queries

board.affected_actor: providers and operators of AI systems (companies)
board.impact: Providers face the highest fine tier under the Regulation, up to 6% of global turnover, for the most serious substantive violations, creating strong deterrent pressure to comply with prohibitions and high-risk data-governance requirements.
board.mechanism: Art 71(3) sets administrative fines of up to 6% of total worldwide annual turnover (or EUR 30 million) for non-compliance with the prohibited practices in Article 5 or the data requirements in Article 10.

evidence.quote: administrative fines of up to 30 000 000 EUR or, if the offender is company, up to 6 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
non-compliance with the prohibition of the artificial intelligence practices referred to in Article 5

board.affected_actor: providers and operators of AI systems (companies)
board.impact: Virtually every substantive obligation in the Regulation beyond Articles 5 and 10 is backed by enforceable fines up to 4% of turnover, giving competent authorities broad enforcement reach even for less severe or documentation-type breaches.
board.mechanism: Art 71(4) establishes a residual fine tier for non-compliance with any requirement or obligation under the Regulation other than those in Articles 5 and 10.

evidence.quote: The non-compliance of the AI system with any requirements or obligations under this Regulation, other than those laid down in Articles 5 and 10, shall be subject to administrative fines of up to 20 000 000 EUR or, if the offender is a company, up to 4 % of its total worldwide annual turnover

board.affected_actor: providers and operators supplying information to notified bodies and competent authorities
board.impact: Operators bear an enforceable duty of accuracy in their dealings with notified bodies and competent authorities, backed by financial penalties independent of the underlying substantive infringement.
board.mechanism: Art 71(5) imposes a distinct fine tier of up to 2% of turnover specifically for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information in response to a request.

evidence.quote: The supply of incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies and national competent authorities in reply to a request shall be subject to administrative fines of up to 10 000 000 EUR or, if the offender is a company, up to 2 % of its total worldwide annual turnover

board.affected_actor: small-scale providers and start-ups facing penalty enforcement
board.impact: Small providers benefit from a structurally more lenient penalty regime than larger operators, reducing their relative enforcement risk exposure for equivalent infringements.
board.mechanism: Art 71(1) directs Member States to take particular account of small-scale providers' and start-ups' interests and economic viability when laying down penalty rules, and Art 71(6)(c) requires authorities to weigh the offender's size and market share when setting individual fine amounts.

evidence.quote: They shall take into particular account the interests of small-scale providers and start-up and their economic viability.
the size and market share of the operator committing the infringement

board.affected_actor: Member States
board.impact: Member States incur a recurring, open-ended notification duty to the Commission each time national penalty rules change, creating an ongoing administrative link between national enforcement and Union-level oversight.
board.mechanism: Art 71(2) requires Member States to notify the Commission of their penalty rules and measures and of any subsequent amendment without delay.

evidence.quote: The Member States shall notify the Commission of those rules and of those measures and shall notify it, without delay, of any subsequent amendment affecting them.

board.affected_actor: public authorities and bodies established in Member States
board.impact: Whether public-sector AI operators face the same fine exposure as private companies is left to national discretion, creating a potential enforcement gap and cross-Member-State divergence for public bodies.
board.mechanism: Art 71(7) leaves it to each Member State to lay down rules on whether and to what extent administrative fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in its territory.

evidence.quote: Each Member State shall lay down rules on whether and to what extent administrative fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in that Member State.

board.affected_actor: national courts and other bodies designated under Member State legal systems
board.impact: Institutional enforcement architecture for fines varies by Member State legal tradition (administrative versus judicial imposition), which may produce differing procedural safeguards and timelines for the same substantive penalty regime across the Union.
board.mechanism: Art 71(8) allows fines to be applied by competent national courts or other bodies depending on the Member State's legal system, provided this has equivalent effect.

evidence.quote: Depending on the legal system of the Member States, the rules on administrative fines may be applied in such a manner that the fines are imposed by competent national courts of other bodies as applicable in those Member States.

board.affected_actor: providers and start-ups participating in AI regulatory sandboxes
board.impact: Participants incur recurring staffing costs to operate under continuous competent-authority supervision and to maintain rapid risk-mitigation capability for the duration of sandbox participation.
board.mechanism: Art 53(1) places sandbox testing under the direct supervision and guidance of competent authorities pursuant to a specific plan, and Art 53(3) requires immediate mitigation (or suspension) of any significant health, safety or fundamental rights risk identified during testing.

evidence.quote: This shall take place under the direct supervision and guidance by the competent authorities with a view to ensuring compliance with the requirements of this Regulation
Any significant risks to health and safety and fundamental rights identified during the development and testing of such systems shall result in immediate mitigation

board.affected_actor: providers and start-ups participating in AI regulatory sandboxes
board.impact: Sandbox participants retain unmitigated civil liability cost exposure for harm caused to third parties by their experimentation, meaning sandbox status confers no financial risk shield.
board.mechanism: Art 53(4) explicitly preserves participants' liability under applicable Union and Member State liability legislation for harm inflicted on third parties from sandbox experimentation.

evidence.quote: Participants in the AI regulatory sandbox shall remain liable under applicable Union and Member States liability legislation for any harm inflicted on third parties as a result from the experimentation taking place in the sandbox.

board.affected_actor: Member State competent authorities hosting AI regulatory sandboxes
board.impact: Hosting authorities face a recurring administrative burden and must build coordination/reporting capacity to fulfil annual reporting to the Board and Commission and cross-authority cooperation duties.
board.mechanism: Art 53(5) requires competent authorities that establish sandboxes to coordinate within the European Artificial Intelligence Board and to submit annual reports to the Board and the Commission on implementation results.

evidence.quote: shall coordinate their activities and cooperate within the framework of the European Artificial Intelligence Board. They shall submit annual reports to the Board and the Commission on the results from the implementation of those scheme

board.affected_actor: sandbox participants processing personal data for public-interest AI development
board.impact: Qualifying participants must make one-off and recurring investments in dedicated data-governance infrastructure (isolated environments, access controls, long-term log retention, documentation and public disclosure) to lawfully reuse personal data in the sandbox.
board.mechanism: Art 54(1)(d),(h),(i),(j) conditions the personal-data reuse exception on maintaining a functionally separate and access-controlled data environment, retaining processing logs for the sandbox duration plus one year, keeping detailed technical documentation, and publishing a project summary.

evidence.quote: any personal data to be processed in the context of the sandbox are in a functionally separate, isolated and protected data processing environment under the control of the participants and only authorised persons have access to that data
the logs of the processing of personal data in the context of the sandbox are kept for the duration of the participation in the sandbox and 1 year after its termination

board.affected_actor: sandbox participants processing personal data for public-interest AI development
board.impact: Participants must staff and operate continuous real-time monitoring and rapid-response functions for the entire duration of sandbox participation, representing an ongoing operational cost rather than a one-off setup expense.
board.mechanism: Art 54(1)(c) conditions the exception on the existence of effective monitoring mechanisms to identify emerging high risks to data subjects' fundamental rights and response mechanisms to promptly mitigate or stop processing.

evidence.quote: there are effective monitoring mechanisms to identify if any high risks to the fundamental rights of the data subjects may arise during the sandbox experimentation as well as response mechanism to promptly mitigate those risks and, where necessary, stop the processing

board.affected_actor: small-scale providers and start-ups
board.impact: Small providers benefit from a direct fee-based cost offset that lowers their conformity-assessment expenditure relative to larger competitors facing standard fees.
board.mechanism: Art 55(2) requires Member States to take small-scale providers' interests and needs into account when setting Art 43 conformity assessment fees, reducing those fees proportionately to size and market size.

evidence.quote: The specific interests and needs of the small-scale providers shall be taken into account when setting the fees for conformity assessment under Article 43, reducing those fees proportionately to their size and market size.

board.affected_actor: small-scale providers and start-ups
board.impact: Priority sandbox access reduces small providers' market-entry cost disadvantage by securing earlier access to supervised testing relative to larger competitors, subject to meeting eligibility conditions.
board.mechanism: Art 55(1)(a) obliges Member States to provide small-scale providers and start-ups with priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes where eligibility conditions are met.

evidence.quote: provide small-scale providers and start-ups with priority access to the AI regulatory sandboxes to the extent that they fulfil the eligibility conditions

board.affected_actor: providers of AI systems subject to the Regulation
board.impact: Providers face tiered administrative fine exposure of up to 6%, 4% or 2% of worldwide annual turnover depending on infringement type, representing a major financial risk that must be factored into compliance cost-benefit decisions.
board.mechanism: Art 71(3)-(5) sets differentiated maximum administrative fines calibrated to the severity of the infringement, expressed as the higher of a fixed euro amount or a percentage of global turnover.

evidence.quote: administrative fines of up to 30 000 000 EUR or, if the offender is company, up to 6 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
administrative fines of up to 20 000 000 EUR or, if the offender is a company, up to 4 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher

board.affected_actor: small-scale providers and start-ups
board.impact: Small providers benefit from reduced relative fine exposure compared to larger competitors facing the same infringement, because penalty-setting must weigh their economic viability.
board.mechanism: Art 71(1) requires that penalty rules take particular account of the interests of small-scale providers and start-ups and their economic viability when penalties are set and applied.

evidence.quote: They shall take into particular account the interests of small-scale providers and start-up and their economic viability.

board.affected_actor: Member State authorities responsible for penalty regimes
board.impact: Member States bear a recurring administrative burden to notify the Commission of their penalty rules and to report any subsequent amendments without delay, adding an ongoing compliance-monitoring cost at national level.
board.mechanism: Art 71(2) requires Member States to notify the Commission of national penalty rules and measures and to notify without delay any subsequent amendment affecting them.

evidence.quote: The Member States shall notify the Commission of those rules and of those measures and shall notify it, without delay, of any subsequent amendment affecting them.

board.affected_actor: providers and start-ups participating in AI regulatory sandboxes
board.impact: Creates a dense set of recurring operational and staffing duties that participants must maintain for the entire duration of sandbox participation, which is likely to be disproportionately costly for resource-constrained small providers and start-ups.
board.mechanism: Article 54(1)(c)-(j) conditions the personal-data reuse exception on maintaining continuous risk-monitoring mechanisms, a functionally isolated data environment, one-year log retention after termination, detailed technical documentation, and a published project summary.

evidence.quote: there are effective monitoring mechanisms to identify if any high risks to the fundamental rights of the data subjects may arise during the sandbox experimentation
the logs of the processing of personal data in the context of the sandbox are kept for the duration of the participation in the sandbox and 1 year after its termination
complete and detailed description of the process and rationale behind the training, testing and validation of the AI system is kept together with the testing results

board.affected_actor: national competent authorities hosting AI regulatory sandboxes
board.impact: Requires authorities to build and sustain continuous technical monitoring capacity for each ongoing sandbox, which may strain the resources of smaller or less well-equipped Member State authorities relative to larger, better-resourced ones.
board.mechanism: Article 53(1) and (3) require the hosting authority to provide direct supervision and guidance throughout the sandbox and to identify and ensure immediate mitigation or suspension of any significant risks to health, safety or fundamental rights arising during testing.

evidence.quote: This shall take place under the direct supervision and guidance by the competent authorities with a view to ensuring compliance with the requirements of this Regulation

Any significant risks to health and safety and fundamental rights identified during the development and testing of such systems shall result in immediate mitigation and, failing that, in the suspension of the development and testing process

board.affected_actor: AI developers pursuing purposes outside the enumerated public-interest areas (e.g. commercially-oriented start-ups)
board.impact: Excludes innovators developing AI for other, non-listed purposes from accessing real personal data in the sandbox, channeling this testing advantage toward public-interest-aligned developers and disadvantaging purely commercial applicants.
board.mechanism: Article 54(1)(a) restricts the personal-data reuse exception to AI systems developed for safeguarding substantial public interest in law enforcement/public security, public health, or environmental protection.

evidence.quote: the innovative AI systems shall be developed for safeguarding substantial public interest in one or more of the following areas

board.affected_actor: sandbox participants seeking to invoke the Article 54 personal-data exception
board.impact: Raises the upfront technical and organisational investment needed to qualify for the exception, favoring participants that already possess compliant data infrastructure (often larger or public-sector bodies) over smaller entities that must build such systems from scratch.
board.mechanism: Conditions (d) and (h) require a functionally separate, isolated and protected data processing environment with restricted access, plus a full year of post-termination log retention, before personal-data reuse is lawful.

evidence.quote: any personal data to be processed in the context of the sandbox are in a functionally separate, isolated and protected data processing environment under the control of the participants and only authorised persons have access to that data

board.affected_actor: small-scale providers and start-ups
board.impact: Priority entry does not reduce the operational compliance workload inside the sandbox, so small providers with earlier access may still struggle to sustain the same resource-intensive duties as better-resourced competitors.
board.mechanism: Article 55(1)(a) grants small-scale providers priority access into AI regulatory sandboxes, but the recurring monitoring, isolation, logging and documentation duties of Article 54 apply equally to every participant regardless of size once admitted.

evidence.quote: provide small-scale providers and start-ups with priority access to the AI regulatory sandboxes to the extent that they fulfil the eligibility conditions
there are effective monitoring mechanisms to identify if any high risks to the fundamental rights of the data subjects may arise during the sandbox experimentation

board.affected_actor: small-scale providers
board.impact: Lowers the direct cost of conformity assessment for small providers relative to larger companies, reducing a significant market-entry cost barrier for smaller competitors.
board.mechanism: Article 55(2) requires conformity-assessment fees to take small-scale providers' specific interests and needs into account and to be reduced proportionately to their size and market size.

evidence.quote: The specific interests and needs of the small-scale providers shall be taken into account when setting the fees for conformity assessment under Article 43, reducing those fees proportionately to their size and market size.

board.affected_actor: small-scale providers and start-ups
board.impact: Gives small providers a built-in mitigating factor that lowers their effective risk-adjusted fine exposure compared with large operators facing the same statutory percentage-of-turnover caps for equivalent infringements.
board.mechanism: Article 71(1) requires national penalty rules to take particular account of the interests of small-scale providers and start-ups and their economic viability, and Article 71(6)(c) requires the operator's size and market share to be weighed when setting individual fine amounts.

evidence.quote: They shall take into particular account the interests of small-scale providers and start-up and their economic viability.
the size and market share of the operator committing the infringement

board.affected_actor: large-scale and high-turnover AI providers
board.impact: Reinforces a differentiated penalty burden that is comparatively heavier in absolute and relative terms for large-scale providers than for small-scale competitors committing similar infringements.
board.mechanism: Because Article 71(1) and (6)(c) direct special leniency consideration toward small-scale providers' economic viability without an equivalent mitigating factor for larger operators, fines calculated as a percentage of worldwide turnover fall proportionately harder on large companies.

evidence.quote: administrative fines of up to 30 000 000 EUR or, if the offender is company, up to 6 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
They shall take into particular account the interests of small-scale providers and start-up and their economic viability.

board.affected_actor: sandbox participants whose experiment both harms a third party and breaches a Regulation requirement
board.impact: Exposes such participants to a dual-track financial risk combining potentially large administrative fines with separate civil damages claims for the same incident, an exposure not disclosed by either provision read in isolation.
board.mechanism: Article 53(4) preserves participants' civil liability under applicable Union and Member State law for harm inflicted on third parties from sandbox experimentation, operating independently of the administrative fines of up to 6% of turnover available under Article 71 for the same underlying non-compliance.

evidence.quote: Participants in the AI regulatory sandbox shall remain liable under applicable Union and Member States liability legislation for any harm inflicted on third parties as a result from the experimentation taking place in the sandbox.
administrative fines of up to 30 000 000 EUR or, if the offender is company, up to 6 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher

board.affected_actor: Member State competent authorities that establish AI regulatory sandboxes
board.impact: Creates a recurring reporting burden and constrains national procedural autonomy, potentially creating capacity gaps for smaller authorities and delaying sandbox launches pending centrally-adopted implementing rules.
board.mechanism: Article 53(5) obliges hosting authorities to submit annual reports to the Board and Commission on sandbox implementation results, while Article 53(6) subjects the sandboxes' eligibility, application, selection and exit modalities to Commission implementing acts.

evidence.quote: They shall submit annual reports to the Board and the Commission on the results from the implementation of those scheme, including good practices, lessons learnt and recommendations on their setup

The modalities and the conditions of the operation of the AI regulatory sandboxes, including the eligibility criteria and the procedure for the application, selection, participation and exiting from the sandbox, and the rights and obligations of the participants shall be set out in implementing acts.

board.affected_actor: Member State governments and authorities administering national penalty regimes
board.impact: Imposes an ongoing administrative tracking and notification burden on Member States, and inconsistent timeliness across jurisdictions could create harmonization gaps in the Commission's EU-wide oversight of penalty regimes.
board.mechanism: Article 71(2) requires Member States to notify the Commission of national penalty rules and of any subsequent amendment affecting them without delay.

evidence.quote: The Member States shall notify the Commission of those rules and of those measures and shall notify it, without delay, of any subsequent amendment affecting them.

board.affected_actor: data subjects whose personal data is reused within a sandbox
board.impact: Shields data subjects from direct adverse decisions resulting from sandbox experimentation and limits how long their data is retained, though this protection operates without any requirement for the data subject's consent to the reuse.
board.mechanism: Article 54(1)(f) prohibits sandbox processing of personal data from leading to any measures or decisions affecting the data subjects, and (g) mandates deletion of that data once sandbox participation ends or the retention period expires.

evidence.quote: any processing of personal data in the context of the sandbox do not lead to measures or decisions affecting the data subjects
any personal data processed in the context of the sandbox are deleted once the participation in the sandbox has terminated or the personal data has reached the end of its retention period
